cues.text: An Appeal from Constantinople
By the late eleventh century, the Byzantine Empire was under severe pressure from the Seljuk Turks, who had overrun most of Byzantine Anatolia following their victory at Manzikert in 1071.

In 1095 the Byzantine emperor Alexius I Comnenus sent envoys west asking Pope Urban II for military assistance — help Urban had already begun soliciting support for at an earlier council in Piacenza that same year.
The Council of Clermont

Urban, a former Cluniac monk and disciple of the reforming Pope Gregory VII, convened a council at Clermont , in Auvergne, in November 1095, ostensibly to address Church reform matters such as simony and clerical discipline.
On its final day, unable to fit the assembled crowd inside any building, Urban addressed them in the open air, delivering what would become one of the most consequential speeches in Church history.
The Call to Arms
Though no verbatim transcript survives — five differing chronicler accounts remain — Urban's message appealed to defend Eastern Christians and recover Jerusalem's holy places from Muslim rule.
It also offered a plenary indulgence to those who undertook the journey out of devotion.
According to the Catholic Encyclopedia, Urban was moved by 'the enormous injury that all, clergy or people, brought upon the Christian Faith' at the news of the Turkish advance.
The crowd's response, tradition holds, was the cry Deus vult — 'God wills it.'
Mobilizing Europe
Urban spent the following months traveling through France to preach the crusade personally, while bishops and popular preachers such as Peter the Hermit spread the call across Western Christendom.
An initial, poorly organized 'People's Crusade' set out ahead of the main armies and was largely destroyed in Anatolia.
The main baronial armies — led by figures such as Godfrey of Bouillon, Bohemond of Taranto, and Raymond of Toulouse — assembled and marched east through 1096 and 1097.
The Capture of Jerusalem
After a grueling campaign through Anatolia and Syria, including the long siege of Antioch, the crusader army reached Jerusalem.
It took the city by assault on July 15, 1099, establishing the Crusader States of Outremer, including the Kingdom of Jerusalem.
The Crusader States would endure in various forms until the fall of Acre in 1291.
Legacy

The First Crusade launched a two-century movement that would shape relations between Latin Christendom, Byzantium, and the Islamic world, deepen the fusion of penance, pilgrimage, and holy war in medieval piety, and produce lasting institutions such as the military orders.

It also, together with events like the 1054 schism, left a complicated legacy of mistrust between Eastern and Western Christians that persisted long after Jerusalem itself was lost again to Saladin in 1187.
